title: The Quinoa Revolution!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore quinoa (keen wa), an Andean pseudo-cereal cultivated for thousands of years around Lake Titicaca in Peru and Bolivia. They cover its history, why it is classed as a pseudo-cereal and whole grain, its nutritional profile (complete protein, potassium, gluten-free with some exceptions), how to rinse and cook it (saponin coating), Chuck's cold summer salad recipe, the 2000s export boom led by Sergio Nuñez de Arauco and the price spike, the critique that the boom priced out Andean farmers, a Peruvian household survey study that found little evidence of that, Bolivia's food sovereignty provisions and the biopiracy controversy, land disputes, llama versus sheep fertilizer and crop diversity concerns, and US quinoa farming in California. The episode ends with the hosts tasting Soylent on air and a listener mail segment about Lucius Cornelius Sulla.

segments.title: Opening banter and teaser
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the chilly studio, tease a live taste of Soylent later, and introduce quinoa as a super food.

segments.title: Quinoa origins and history
segments.summary: Quinoa has been cultivated for more than five thousand years and originated in the Andean highlands around Lake Titicaca in Peru and Bolivia; evidence of domestication goes back about eight thousand years. It reached the US in the early twentieth century through USDA efforts, but became popular only in the 2000s, with Oprah's 2008 cleanse helping spread it.

segments.title: Pseudo-cereal and whole grain classification
segments.summary: Quinoa is classed as a pseudo-cereal because it comes from the goosefoot plant rather than a grass. It qualifies as a whole grain since the whole seed is eaten, while refined white flour loses the bran and germ.

segments.title: Quinoa nutrition and protein
segments.summary: Quinoa contains at least ten amino acids and all essential amino acids, making it a complete protein, though it is not exceptionally high in protein compared with legumes. It is low in calories, sugar, cholesterol and sodium, has a lot of potassium, fiber and magnesium, and is commonly described as gluten free, though a few varieties can trigger celiac responses.

segments.title: How to rinse and cook quinoa
segments.summary: The hosts explain that quinoa has a soapy saponin coating that should be rinsed off with a fine sieve until the water runs clear. It is cooked like rice at one part quinoa to two parts liquid, simmered covered until the seed spirals show. Saponin has possible health properties but is bitter and is not eaten.

segments.title: Chuck's cold quinoa salad and recipes
segments.summary: Chuck describes his favorite recipe: cooked quinoa chilled overnight and mixed with cucumber, red onion, peppers, pine nuts, basil, lemon juice and cider vinegar. They also discuss using quinoa in burgers in place of breadcrumbs.

segments.title: Quinoa export boom and Sergio Nuñez de Arauco
segments.summary: US quinoa imports rose sharply in the 2000s. Bolivian UN development worker Sergio Nuñez de Arauco organized indigenous farmers into a cooperative to build a reliable supply for export, and prices rose from about five hundred dollars per metric ton to roughly threefold by around 2010.

segments.title: Hipster backlash and Peruvian household study
segments.summary: Critics argued that Western demand priced Andean farmers out of quinoa and left them malnourished. A study of Peruvian household survey data over ten years, covering 22,000 households, found welfare rose for growers and non-growers alike, and consumption of quinoa in the Puno region did not fall despite a fourfold price increase. Researcher Andrew Stevens was quoted on the findings.

segments.title: Food sovereignty, biopiracy and land disputes
segments.summary: Bolivia's 2009 constitution recognized quinoa under food sovereignty. A Colorado researcher was reportedly killed while smuggling quinoa seeds out of Bolivia, and Colorado State University patented a hybrid based on Bolivian seeds, which Bolivia called biopiracy. Rising value also sparked land grabs and violent disputes over previously abandoned land.

segments.title: Llamas, fallow fields, and crop diversity
segments.summary: Farmers stopped letting fields lie fallow and replaced llama grazing and llama manure, which suits quinoa, with imported sheep manure that brings more pests and weeds. Farmers are also abandoning many of the thousands of local varieties in favor of a few export varieties, which threatens adaptation to climate change. Governments and groups are promoting domestic markets such as school food programs.

segments.title: Quinoa farming in California and wrap-up of topic
segments.summary: Quinoa is being grown in California, including the Sonoran Desert and the Imperial Valley. Quinoa is closely related to lamb's quarters, which is toxic to livestock, and it can carry a virus that harms alfalfa. The hosts joke about possible episode titles.

segments.title: Soylent taste test
segments.summary: The hosts taste Soylent on air for the first time. They describe it as tasting like cereal milk or Cheerios milk, with a chalky aftertaste, and say it is not bad.

segments.title: Listener mail: Sulla and family history
segments.summary: A listener from Sydney writes that her grandmother's maiden name is Sulla, linked to Lucius Cornelius Sulla from the Dictators episode, and that her family is from southern Italy. She also sends a shout out to her sister.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, invite social media contact, and point to the website for more information.
